explain: The 2017 paper by Vaswani et al. introduced the Transformer, eliminating recurrence and convolution and basing everything on attention. The other cited papers cover BERT, GPT, and ResNet.
options: Attention Is All You Need by Vaswani et al., published in 2017
BERT: Pre-training of Deep Bidirectional Transformers, 2018
Language Models are Unsupervised Multitask Learners, 2019
Deep Residual Learning for Image Recognition by He et al., 2015
q: Which paper introduced the original Transformer architecture?
source: paper Attention Is All You Need

explain: RNNs and LSTMs process tokens one at a time in sequence, while the Transformer processes all tokens in parallel thanks to self-attention. This parallelism makes much better use of GPUs.
options: It uses larger recurrent hidden states, processed sequentially just like those of LSTMs
It processes all tokens of the sequence in parallel instead of one at a time in sequence
It replaces backpropagation with a gradient-free evolutionary optimizer
It requires less training data because it does not use learned positional embeddings at all
q: What is the fundamental processing difference between a Transformer and an RNN or LSTM?

explain: The Key matrix acts as the label of each token: it is compared against the Queries via dot product to measure compatibility between tokens. The content being carried lives in the Value instead.
options: To store the tokenizer vocabulary for the final decoding of the text
To hold the final output vector of the model before the classification softmax layer
To act as a label compared against Queries to measure compatibility between tokens
To encode the absolute position of the token in the ordered input sequence
q: In self-attention, what is the role of the Key matrix?

explain: After computing the attention weights with Query and Key, those weights are used to take a weighted average of the Value vectors, which contain the actual informational content of each token.
options: The raw compatibility scores between Query and Key before softmax normalization
The transition probabilities that connect one Transformer layer to the next one
The sinusoidal position vectors that are added to the token embeddings
The informational content aggregated as a weighted average by the attention weights
q: In self-attention, what does the Value matrix represent?

explain: This is the exact scaled dot-product attention formula: QK-transpose product, scaling, softmax, and multiplication by V. The other formulas use wrong functions or operations.
options: Attention(Q,K,V) = softmax(QK transpose / square root of d_k) V
Attention(Q,K,V) = ReLU(QK transpose) + V divided by d_k
Attention(Q,K,V) = sigmoid(Q + K) multiplied by V
Attention(Q,K,V) = softmax(QV transpose / square root of d_model) K
q: What is the correct formula for scaled dot-product attention?
source: paper Attention Is All You Need

explain: The original Transformer used fixed sinusoidal positional encodings, while BERT and GPT-2/GPT-3 use positional embeddings learned during training. RoPE is a more recent technique used by models such as LLaMA.
options: The original Transformer and BERT both use Rotary Embedding (RoPE)
BERT and GPT-2/GPT-3 use positional embeddings learned during training
All modern models use only fixed sinusoids with no exceptions
GPT uses fixed sinusoids while the original Transformer used learned vectors
q: Which models use learned positional embeddings instead of fixed sinusoids?

explain: The FFN is position-wise: the same two-layer linear network with ReLU is applied identically and independently to each position of the sequence. Parameters change from layer to layer but not from position to position.
options: It mixes information across different positions of the sequence, just like self-attention does
It processes each position separately with the same network applied to every token
It concatenates all tokens into a single vector before processing them together
It replaces the softmax computation in the attention-weight block
q: How does the feed-forward network (FFN) operate inside a Transformer layer?
source: paper Attention Is All You Need

explain: Each sub-layer is wrapped with a residual connection and normalization in the form Output = LayerNorm(x + Sublayer(x)), called Post-LN in the original paper. Dropout is applied to the sub-layer output before the sum.
options: BatchNorm(x) with applied dropout and no residual connection at all
Sublayer(x) minus x with normalization computed over the training batch
Only the sum x + Sublayer(x), with no subsequent normalization applied
LayerNorm(x + Sublayer(x)) with residual connection and normalization
q: What is the structure of the Add and Norm block in the original Transformer?
source: paper Attention Is All You Need

explain: The padding mask prevents the model from attending to the filler tokens added to make lengths uniform within a batch. Without it, padding would contaminate the representations.
options: To stop attention from considering the filler tokens added to even out batch lengths
To stop the decoder from looking at future tokens during autoregressive text generation
To zero out the gradients of the normalization layers during model fine-tuning
To randomly mask 15% of tokens as in BERT masked-LM pre-training
q: What is the purpose of the padding mask in self-attention?

explain: The causal (look-ahead) mask zeroes the scores toward future positions so that the token at position i can only attend to tokens up to i. It preserves the autoregressive property in training and generation.
options: It lets the decoder also use right-side context, as BERT does in bidirectional reading
It stops each token from attending to the future, allowing only past and present
It masks padding tokens in short sequences of a mixed training batch
It makes decoder attention bidirectional during autoregressive generation
q: What does the causal mask (look-ahead mask) do in the decoder?

explain: The encoder layer has two sub-layers (self-attention and FFN), while the decoder layer has three because it adds encoder-decoder cross-attention between the masked self-attention and the FFN.
options: Encoder and decoder both have two sub-layers with a fully identical structure
The decoder has two sub-layers and the encoder has three with the cross-attention block
The decoder has three sub-layers because it adds encoder-decoder cross-attention
The encoder has no FFN while the decoder uses two FFNs in parallel with each other
q: How many sub-layers does a decoder layer contain compared to an encoder layer in the original Transformer?
source: paper Attention Is All You Need

explain: In cross-attention the Queries come from the decoder (which is generating) while Key and Value come from the encoder output (which encoded the input). This is how the decoder queries the representation of the input.
options: Query, Key, and Value all come from the decoder, exactly as in self-attention
Query and Key from the encoder and Value from the decoder, purely for symmetry
Query, Key, and Value all come from the encoder, exactly as in self-attention
Query from the decoder while Key and Value come from the encoder output
q: In encoder-decoder cross-attention, where do Query, Key, and Value come from?

explain: BERT is a bidirectional encoder suited to understanding and classification, GPT is an autoregressive decoder suited to generation. T5 and BART are instead full encoder-decoder models.
options: BERT is bidirectional encoder-only, GPT is autoregressive decoder-only
BERT and GPT are both full encoder-decoder models for machine translation
BERT is causal decoder-only and GPT is encoder-only with bidirectional masking
BERT and GPT both use cross-attention with no internal self-attention
q: Which statement correctly describes BERT versus GPT?

explain: The QK-transpose score matrix has size n by n, so time and memory grow quadratically with the sequence length n. This is the bottleneck for long contexts.
options: Linear O(n) in both compute time and activation memory together
Quadratic O(n^2) in time and memory with respect to sequence length
Constant O(1), fully independent of the processed sequence length
Proportional only to the vocabulary size of the language model
q: What is the computational complexity of standard self-attention with respect to the sequence length n?

explain: In the base model d_model is 512, and with 8 heads each one works on d_k = d_v = 512/8 = 64 dimensions. This is the standard configuration of the original paper.
options: d_model 256 with 4 heads of 32 dimensions each
d_model 1024 with 16 heads of 128 dimensions each
d_model 512 with 8 heads of 64 dimensions each
d_model 768 with 12 heads of 96 dimensions each
q: In the base Transformer of the original paper, what are the embedding size and the size of each head?
source: paper Attention Is All You Need

explain: Parallelism over all tokens keeps the parallel compute units of GPUs saturated, unlike intrinsically sequential RNNs. This drastically reduces training times on long sequences.
options: It completely removes the need for large annotated training datasets
It reduces the number of parameters compared to an RNN of equal capacity
It makes the model interpretable by inspecting a single weight per token
It exploits GPU parallel computation by processing all tokens together
q: What is the main practical advantage of Transformer parallelism on GPUs compared to RNNs?

explain: In self-attention every token is directly connected to every other in a single step, so the maximum distance between tokens is O(1). In RNNs the signal must cross O(n) sequential steps, degrading over long distances.
options: The maximum distance between any tokens is a single O(1) step, versus O(n) steps in RNNs
The number of model parameters grows linearly with the processed sequence length
Gradients can never explode or vanish thanks to the total absence of recurrent connections
Each token can only attend to the token immediately preceding it in the sequence
q: Why does self-attention model long-range dependencies better than RNNs?

explain: Without scaling, with large d_k the dot products take very large values in magnitude and push the softmax into saturated regions where gradients are almost zero. Dividing by the square root of d_k keeps unit variance and stable gradients.
options: To reduce the parameters of the attention matrix from O(n^2) to linear O(n)
Large dot products would saturate the softmax and zero out the gradients
To make the sum of attention weights equal d_k instead of 1 as per softmax
To add non-linearity to the compatibility-score computation between tokens
q: What is the main consequence of NOT dividing by the square root of d_k when d_k is large?
source: paper Attention Is All You Need

explain: If the query and key components are independent with zero mean and unit variance, the variance of their dot product equals d_k. Scaling brings the variance back to about 1, statistically justifying the division.
options: The mean of the dot product grows as the square of d_k
The norm of the Value vectors halves at each successive Transformer layer
The variance of the dot product equals d_k, and scaling brings it back to about 1
The standard deviation of the softmax weights after training always equals d_k
q: Assuming independent zero-mean, unit-variance components, why is scaling by the square root of d_k statistically justified?

explain: The outputs of the h heads are concatenated and then reprojected with the W^O matrix to return to d_model size. Without this projection the dimensions would not match the rest of the layer.
options: They are added element-wise with no subsequent linear projection in the layer
Only the head with the highest average score is kept and all the rest are discarded
They are multiplied together to obtain a single shared attention matrix
They are concatenated and reprojected with an output matrix W^O to d_model size
q: What happens to the outputs of the individual heads in multi-head attention?
source: paper Attention Is All You Need

explain: The standard convention is d_k = d_v = d_model / h, hence 512/8 = 64. This keeps the total compute cost comparable to a single full head but with greater expressiveness.
options: Each head works on 64 dimensions, given by 512 divided by 8
Each head works on 512 independent dimensions for a total of 4096
Each head works on 8 dimensions, given by 64 divided by 8
The head size is independent of d_model and always equals 32
q: With d_model 512 and 8 heads, how many dimensions does each head work on under the standard convention?
source: paper Attention Is All You Need

explain: Self-attention treats the input as an unordered set: it is permutation-invariant. Without positional information, sentences with the same words in a different order would be indistinguishable to the model.
options: The model would become insensitive to order, treating each sentence as an unordered set
The attention weights would all become zero and the model output would be identically zero
The model would need twice the parameters to still manage to converge
Computational complexity would become cubic instead of quadratic in the sequence
q: What would happen if positional encoding were completely removed from a Transformer?

explain: The positional encoding has the same d_model size as the token embeddings, so it can be added element-wise. The sum fuses semantic and positional information without increasing dimensions.
options: It is concatenated to the embeddings, doubling the size to 2 times d_model
It is multiplied by the Value matrix before the softmax computation
It is added to the token embeddings, having the same d_model size
It is used in place of the token embeddings with no combination
q: How is positional encoding combined with input embeddings in the original Transformer?
source: paper Attention Is All You Need

explain: Absolute positional encoding encodes the exact position of the token (e.g. position 5); relative encoding encodes the distance between pairs of tokens (e.g. i-j = 3). Relative methods such as RoPE generalize better to long sequences.
options: The absolute one is added to token embeddings, while the relative one replaces the softmax
The absolute one serves only the causal decoder, the relative one only the encoder
There is no difference at all: they are two names for the exact same technique
The absolute one encodes the token position, the relative one the distance between tokens
q: What is the difference between absolute and relative positional encoding?

explain: The identity path y = x + Sublayer(x) offers gradients a direct route through deep layers, mitigating the vanishing-gradient problem. The sub-layer only has to learn the residual, an easier optimization task.
options: They give gradients a direct path along the identity route, mitigating vanishing
They reduce attention complexity from quadratic to linear in sequence length
They completely remove the need for positional encoding in very deep models
They freeze the weights of the first network layers to speed up fine-tuning
q: Why are residual connections essential for training deep Transformers?

explain: LayerNorm computes mean and variance over the features of a single token, so it is batch-independent. BatchNorm depends on batch statistics, which are unstable with variable-length sequences and the small batches typical of NLP.
options: BatchNorm is not differentiable and therefore blocks backpropagation in deep layers
Sequences vary in length with unstable batch statistics; LayerNorm operates per token
LayerNorm introduces many more parameters and hence greater model expressiveness
BatchNorm only works on images, never on tokenized natural-language text
q: Why do Transformers use LayerNorm instead of BatchNorm?

explain: The original paper uses Post-LN (LayerNorm after the residual sum), while later models such as GPT-2 adopt Pre-LN (normalization before the sub-layer) because it is more stable with very deep networks and high learning rates.
options: They are fully equivalent and the choice is purely cosmetic, with no effect on training
Post-LN removes the residuals and Pre-LN removes layer normalization entirely
The paper uses Post-LN after the sum; modern models use Pre-LN, more stable in depth
Pre-LN normalizes the batch of examples, Post-LN normalizes the single dense layer of the block
q: What is the difference between Post-LN and Pre-LN in Transformers?

explain: The padding mask hides batch filler tokens, the causal mask hides future positions to preserve autoregressivity. They serve different purposes and can coexist in the decoder during training.
options: They are identical and freely interchangeable in any existing Transformer architecture
The padding mask serves the decoder and the causal mask only the encoder
The causal mask zeroes gradients while the padding mask amplifies them in training
The padding mask hides filler tokens, the causal mask hides future positions
q: What is the difference between a padding mask and a causal mask?

explain: Without a causal mask the model would see future tokens during training (information leakage) and learn to cheat instead of predicting. At generation time it would still be forced to proceed left to right.
options: It would peek at future tokens in training, invalidating autoregressive learning
It would become faster in training with no loss at all in final model quality
Complexity would drop from quadratic to linear in a fully automatic and free way
Nothing would change because the mask is only ever used during inference
q: What would happen if the causal mask were removed from a GPT decoder during training?

explain: In translation the encoder encodes the whole source sentence and the decoder generates the translation by consulting that encoding via cross-attention. This is the original use case of the 2017 paper.
options: Classifying single sentences with a compact and efficient bidirectional encoder model
Machine translation, with an encoder that encodes and a decoder that generates
Free text generation with no external conditioning input to the model at all
Image recognition with no textual component associated with the system
q: For which task is the full encoder-decoder architecture the most natural choice?
source: paper Attention Is All You Need

explain: Quadratic cost limits the maximum processable length, defining the context window of the model. Going beyond it requires truncation or efficient techniques such as sliding window or sparse attention.
options: The vocabulary size must always stay smaller than the processed sequence length
The context window is limited by quadratic cost: beyond it, truncation or efficient attention is needed
The number of heads must grow linearly with the processed sequence length
Sinusoidal positional encoding stops working entirely beyond 100 context tokens
q: How does O(n^2) complexity constrain the context window of a model?

explain: In the base model the FFN expands from 512 to 2048 with the first linear layer and projects back to 512 with the second, with ReLU in between. The intermediate expansion gives the model capacity.
options: From 512 to 64 and back to 512 with hyperbolic tangent
From 512 to 512 with no intermediate expansion and no activation
From 2048 to 512 and back to 2048 with sigmoid
From 512 to 2048 and back to 512 with ReLU in between
q: What sizes does the FFN use in the base Transformer of the original paper?
source: paper Attention Is All You Need

explain: Attention communicates across positions (mixing information along the sequence); the FFN computes inside each position, adding non-linearity and capacity. Without the FFN, attention would be almost only a weighted linear combination.
options: Attention mixes information across positions, FFN processes within each position
The FFN mixes information across positions while attention normalizes the batch instead
They are interchangeable and modern models keep only one of them, chosen at random
Attention only works in training while the FFN only works in inference
q: What is the division of roles between attention and FFN in a Transformer layer?

explain: In self-attention Q, K, and V all derive from the same sequence via different projections. In cross-attention only the Queries come from the decoder, while Key and Value come from the encoder output.
options: They are identical in every way: in both cases Q, K, and V all come from the same token sequence
Self-attention: Q, K, V from the same sequence; cross-attention: Query from decoder, rest from encoder
In self-attention the Value matrix is missing entirely and is added only in cross-attention
In cross-attention Query and Key come from the encoder and Value comes from the decoder
q: How does the derivation of Q, K, and V differ between self-attention and cross-attention?

explain: The masked formula adds a matrix M to the scores before the softmax, with M equal to zero on allowed positions and minus infinity on forbidden ones. The softmax thus zeroes the weights of masked positions.
options: The scores of forbidden positions are multiplied by zero right after the softmax computation step
Forbidden tokens are physically removed from the sequence before every single layer
A matrix with zeros on allowed and minus infinity on forbidden positions is added to the scores
Gaussian noise is added to the scores of the positions to mask in the training batch
q: How is an attention mask implemented mathematically in the scores?

explain: For classification and understanding (sentiment, NER, extractive QA) a bidirectional encoder such as BERT exploits both left and right context. A causal decoder would waste half of the context available for these tasks.
options: A causal decoder-only model because it generates one token at a time in a natural autoregressive way
A full encoder-decoder model because intermediate cross-attention is always needed
A bag-of-words model without attention to reduce training costs
A bidirectional encoder-only model, which exploits left and right context in classification
q: A team must pick a model to classify reviews and recognize named entities. Which architecture fits best, and why?

explain: Chatbot generation requires an autoregressive decoder with a causal mask: each token is generated conditioned only on the past. A bidirectional encoder could not generate in a natural autoregressive way.
options: An autoregressive decoder-only model with causal mask, generating conditioned on the past
A bidirectional encoder-only model, because generation benefits from future context
A model without positional encoding, because token order does not matter in dialogue
An encoder-decoder model without masks, because masks always slow down inference
q: A team must build a chatbot that generates replies token by token. Which architecture fits best, and why?

explain: With quadratic cost, doubling n from 2048 to 4096 multiplies time and memory by 4 (2 squared). That is why doubling the context window costs so much in GPU memory.
options: Only the occupied memory doubles while compute time stays unchanged
The cost stays unchanged thanks to the massive parallelism of modern GPUs
Training time halves due to batching over long sequences
Time and memory roughly quadruple because of the quadratic dependency
q: A team doubles the sequence length from 2048 to 4096 tokens. What happens to the self-attention cost?

explain: With large d_k, dot products have large magnitude, the softmax saturates by assigning almost all weight to a single token, and gradients become tiny. Scaling keeps the logits in a regime where the softmax can learn.
options: The softmax would produce almost uniform weights and the model would become a bag-of-words
The attention weights would exceed 1, violating the probabilistic normalization of the softmax
The softmax saturates on a single token with near-zero gradients, halting learning
The QK-transpose matrix would no longer be square and the matrix product would fail
q: With very large d_k and no scaling, which phenomenon blocks learning in the attention softmax?
source: paper Attention Is All You Need

explain: RoPE rotates the Query and Key representations as a function of absolute position, so their dot product depends only on the relative distance between tokens. It combines the benefits of absolute and relative encoding and is used by LLaMA and Mistral.
options: It adds fixed sinusoids to embeddings exactly as in the original 2017 Transformer
It learns a distinct positional vector for each position, exactly as BERT does
It concatenates absolute position as an extra feature right before the layer FFN
It rotates Query and Key with position, so the product depends on relative distance
q: How does Rotary Positional Embedding (RoPE), used by models such as LLaMA, work?

explain: In autoregressive generation the KV-cache stores the Key and Value of already-processed tokens so they are not recomputed at each step. Without the cache, each new token would cost a quadratic reprocessing of the whole sequence.
options: It stores past tokens Key and Value so they are not recomputed at each step
It stores all gradients locally to resume training after an interruption
It compresses all model weights via 4-bit quantization during inference
It saves the whole tokenizer vocabulary in the serving-server GPU memory
q: A team optimizes LLM inference and introduces the KV-cache. Which problem does it solve?

explain: Sinusoids are deterministic functions defined for any position, so the model can extrapolate beyond the lengths seen in training. Learned embeddings exist only for seen positions and fail past the maximum trained length.
options: They require more parameters and hence implicitly store more context in a stable way
They are deterministic for every position and allow extrapolation beyond training
They have an intrinsically infinite context window with no extra compute cost
They completely eliminate the quadratic complexity of self-attention on long sequences
q: What theoretical advantage does sinusoidal positional encoding have over learned ones on sequences longer than training?
source: paper Attention Is All You Need

explain: The FFN with an expanded intermediate layer and non-linearity adds the computational capacity that attention alone lacks, attention being largely a linear weighted average. Studies interpret it as key-value memory distributed in the weights.
options: It directly computes the attention weights while attention normalizes the example batch
It only serves to reduce parameters and could be removed with no practical effect
It adds non-linearity inside each position, like a learned key-value memory
It replaces positional encoding in models with more than 12 deep layers
q: Why is the FFN indispensable even though attention already mixes information across tokens?

explain: The trap is confusing the roles: the encoder uses no causal mask and is bidirectional, the decoder uses one and is causal. The padding mask, instead, can appear in both to handle batching.
options: The causal mask is used only in the encoder and never in the autoregressive decoder
The padding mask always replaces the causal mask inside the causal decoder
Encoder and decoder both use only bidirectional attention with no mask at all
The encoder is bidirectional with no causal mask, the decoder uses a causal autoregressive mask
q: Which statement about masks in encoder and decoder is correct? Watch out for the typical exam trap.

explain: In the decoder during training both are needed: the causal mask preserves autoregressivity and the padding mask excludes batch filler. Applying only one would leave a hole: either leakage from the future or contamination from padding.
options: Apply padding and causal masks together: one excludes filler, the other the future
Use only the padding mask because the causal mask is obsolete in modern efficient models
Remove all masks because they always slow down distributed training on GPUs
Use only the causal mask because padding never influences model gradients
q: A chatbot in training processes batches with different-length sequences in a causal decoder. Which masking strategy is correct?

explain: The Query represents what the token is looking for: it is compared against all Keys to decide which tokens to attend to. The actual content to aggregate lives in the Value instead.
options: To carry the informational content aggregated as a weighted average by the weights
To represent what the token is looking for, compared against the Keys
To encode the absolute position of the token in the sequence
To hold the final layer output before the FFN
q: In self-attention, what is the role of a token Query vector?

explain: The softmax normalizes the scores of one token toward all others, so the sum is always 1: the weights form a probability distribution over the whole sequence.
options: It equals d_k, the Key size used for scaling the attention scores
It equals the number of heads of the multi-head attention module
It equals 1, like a probability distribution over the sequence
It equals 0 in practice, because masks zero out all the scores
q: After the softmax, what is the sum of a token attention weights toward all others?

explain: BPE starts from individual characters and merges the most frequent adjacent pair at each step, until reaching the desired vocabulary size. This is the method used by the GPT family.
options: It masks 15% of tokens as in BERT pre-training
It assigns a learned vector to each sequence position
It rotates Query and Key as a function of the distance between tokens
It starts from characters and merges the most frequent adjacent pairs
q: How does Byte Pair Encoding (BPE) build its vocabulary?

explain: BPE merges the most frequent pairs, while WordPiece chooses merges that maximize likelihood and marks continuations with ## (e.g. un + ##believ + ##able). Both solve the out-of-vocabulary problem.
options: They are the same algorithm with two names and an identical final vocabulary
WordPiece marks continuations with ## and merges by likelihood
BPE uses the ## prefix while WordPiece only works at word level
WordPiece does not handle unseen words, while BPE discards them entirely
q: Which statement distinguishes WordPiece (BERT) from BPE?

explain: A small vocabulary fragments each word into many pieces and lengthens sequences; a huge one inflates the embedding matrix and leaves rare tokens almost never trained. The choice is a trade-off between length and coverage.
options: Small stretches sequences, large inflates embeddings and leaves rare tokens
Vocabulary size affects neither sequences nor learned parameters
A larger vocabulary is always better, with no downside or cost
A smaller vocabulary is always better, with no downside or cost
q: What does a tokenization vocabulary that is too small or too large imply?

explain: The encoder uses no causal mask: each token attends both left and right, building representations that incorporate the whole sentence context in both directions.
options: Each token attends left and right, with no causal mask on the future
Each token attends only to the past like in a causal autoregressive decoder
It uses cross-attention toward a second external support encoder
It processes one token at a time in sequence like a classic RNN
q: Why is the Transformer encoder called bidirectional?

explain: T5 and BART keep full encoders and decoders linked by cross-attention: the encoder encodes the document, the decoder generates the summary or translation by consulting it step by step.
options: They are pure decoder-only models optimized for single short-reply chatbots
They are encoder-only with classification on top of the final [CLS] token
They are full encoder-decoder models, ideal for summaries and translations
They use no attention but only very deep feed-forward networks
q: Which architecture do T5 and BART use, and which tasks is it designed for?

explain: In image captioning a visual encoder produces the image features and the text decoder queries them: Queries arise from the text being generated, Key and Value from the regions of the encoded image.
options: Query, Key, and Value all come from the pixels of the original input image
Cross-attention is never used in any modern multimodal model
Query and Key from the image and Value from the text generated so far
Query from the text decoder, Key and Value from the encoded visual features
q: In an image captioning model, how are Query, Key, and Value distributed in cross-attention?

explain: Each head projects the same input with three different learned matrices (W_Q, W_K, W_V): from a single sequence three different views arise — one for searching, one for being found, one for carrying content.
options: From learned projections of the input, with W_Q, W_K, and W_V matrices per head
From three different input sequences fed separately to the model all together
From fixed random vectors that stay unchanged during the whole training
From splitting the positional encoding into three equal-sized components
q: Where do Q, K, and V come from inside an attention head?

explain: Independent projections let each head specialize: one may track syntactic relations, another coreferences between pronouns and nouns, yet another long-range dependencies.
options: To double the parameters without changing the behavior of the model
To process several different batches in parallel on the same GPU
So each head observes a different subspace and can specialize
To make the overall complexity linear in the sequence length
q: Why does each attention head have its own independent projection matrices?

explain: Attention dropout randomly zeroes some weights after the softmax during training: it stops heads from co-adapting and from always depending on the same tokens, improving generalization.
options: To speed up inference by skipping the final softmax computation in each head
To regularize by randomly zeroing some weights during training
To mask padding tokens in mixed-length batches
To stop the decoder from observing future tokens in generation
q: What is attention dropout for in the Transformer?

explain: The original positional encoding alternates sine on even dimensions and cosine on odd ones, with decreasing frequencies according to the denominator 10000 raised to 2i/d_model. It is fixed and deterministic for each position.
options: Sine on even and cosine on odd dimensions, with decreasing frequencies
Sigmoid on all dimensions with the very same identical frequency
Learned random vectors that differ at each model training epoch
ReLU applied to the absolute position divided by d_model
q: Which functions does the sinusoidal positional encoding of the original paper use?

explain: The geometrically progressing wavelengths from 2 pi to 10000 times 2 pi assign each position a unique fingerprint: high frequencies distinguish nearby positions, low frequencies capture distances and relative shifts.
options: To reduce the number of parameters compared to learned embeddings
To make the model fully invariant to the input token order
To give each position a unique fingerprint and capture relative distances
To zero out the gradients of all positions beyond 512 tokens
q: Why do the positional-encoding sinusoids use different frequencies per dimension?

explain: Greedy picks the most likely token at each single step and can fall into local optima; beam search keeps the k best partial sequences and often finds an overall more likely sentence, at the cost of more compute.
options: Greedy takes the best token at each step, beam keeps the k best sequences
Beam search is deterministic while greedy is always stochastic and varies each run
Greedy requires more memory than beam search for the same model
They are identical when the sampling temperature equals 1
q: What is the difference between greedy decoding and beam search in generation?

explain: Temperature divides the logits before the softmax: high values flatten the distribution and make output more varied and creative, low values concentrate it on the best tokens; at the zero-temperature limit you get greedy decoding.
options: It counts the number of generated tokens before automatic stopping of the generated sequence
High flattens the distribution and increases variety, low concentrates it
It multiplies the number of attention heads during inference
It normalizes gradients to prevent explosion in training
q: What does temperature control in LLM sampling?

explain: Top-k truncates to a fixed number of candidates, rigid when the distribution is flat or peaked; top-p selects the smallest group covering probability p, adapting the candidate count to the shape of the distribution step by step.
options: Top-k sorts by position in the sequence, top-p sorts by frequency seen in training
Top-p exists only in training, while top-k is used only in inference
Top-k keeps a fixed number of tokens, top-p the smallest group covering probability p
Top-k raises the sampling temperature, top-p raises the maximum output length

explain: The FFN contains two large dense matrices (d_model by d_ff and back) per layer: about two thirds of model parameters live there, not in the attention matrices. That is also why the FFN is seen as distributed memory.
options: In the Query, Key, and Value matrices of each deep layer self-attention
In the FFN, with the two dense expansion and projection matrices
In the fixed sinusoidal positional encoding of the first layer
In the embedding matrix of the padding token
q: Where do most parameters of a Transformer layer live?

explain: Each generated token adds its own Key and Value in every layer, so the cache grows linearly with length; the dominant memory factor is the product of layer count, length, and head size.
options: It stays constant because old tokens are overwritten by new ones
It shrinks because early tokens get progressively compressed
It grows quadratically by recomputing everything at each step
It grows linearly: each token adds one K/V pair per layer
q: How does KV-cache memory grow with the length of the generated sequence?

explain: With learned positional embeddings only the positions seen in training exist: past the maximum trained length the model has no positional references and quality collapses. Truncation, sliding windows, or extrapolation techniques are needed.
options: It meets never-seen positions and degrades: truncation or extrapolation is needed
It keeps working perfectly up to infinite length with no limits
It crashes with an error because attention requires short sequences
It automatically improves because a wider window always helps the model in every case
q: What happens if inference exceeds the maximum length seen in training?

explain: Without positional information, attention depends only on content: permuting the input tokens permutes outputs and weights accordingly. Order becomes invisible and anagram sentences look identical.
options: Attention weights all become zero and the model output is always zero
Computational complexity goes from quadratic to cubic in the sequence
Permuting the input permutes the output the same way: order is invisible
Each token can then only attend to itself and to no other token at all
q: Self-attention without positional encoding is permutation-equivariant. What does that mean in practice?

explain: Each layer transforms the representations of the previous one: early layers capture local syntax, deep ones semantics and abstract relations. Residual connections make this depth optimizable, which is impossible for a single wide layer.
options: To increase the distributed batch size across multiple modern GPUs
To reduce the memory occupied by the KV-cache during inference
To compose ever more abstract representations, made optimizable by residuals
To remove entirely the need for normalization between blocks
